summary: Voltage, current, resistance and power are linked by Ohm's law; safe practice means a low-voltage supply, ESD protection and correct polarity.
Passive components (resistors, capacitors, inductors) store or dissipate energy; their values are read from colour bands or printed codes.
Active components (diodes, LEDs, BJTs, MOSFETs, ICs) switch and amplify; CMOS gates are built from complementary MOSFET pairs and NAND is universal.
Connectors, switches, relays, buzzers and crystals complete a circuit; datasheets give ratings, pinouts and packages.
A multimeter, component tester and ESR meter distinguish good parts from faulty ones, and parts must be tested out of circuit.

units.title: Introduction to Networking Components
topics: Eight rules for handling network hardware

sections.title: Eight rules for handling network hardware

summary: Network devices are placed by layer: modem and NIC at the physical link, hub at layer 1, switch and AP at layer 2, router at layer 3.
UTP is the standard LAN cable up to 100 m; Cat5e and Cat6 are used for Gigabit, Cat6a for 10 Gbps.
Straight-through, crossover and rollover cables differ only in pin order; T568B is the usual choice and Auto-MDI/MDI-X has made crossover cables rare.
Coaxial serves cable TV and legacy bus networks; fibre gives distance and immunity to interference.
Testing begins at layer 1 with link lights and a cable tester, and every fix goes in the log.

summary: Protect yourself and the parts: unplug, discharge static, never open a PSU.
The toolkit is small and cheap; a multimeter, crimper and a bootable USB solve most jobs.
Every component has a few specifications that decide compatibility and performance.
Simple arithmetic selects the PSU, UPS and storage layout and explains real speeds and capacities.

sections.title: Eight common assembly mistakes and how to avoid them

Drivers, updates, printer installation and basic maintenance after installing the OS
Eight tips for a safe operating-system installation

summary: Build in a fixed order, handling the CPU and RAM carefully and tightening screws evenly.
Front-panel headers need the manual; LEDs have polarity, switches do not.
Check twice before power-on: no loose screws, all power connected, monitor on the right port.
If it fails, use beep codes, debug LEDs and a minimum-configuration test to isolate the part.
UEFI replaces BIOS and brings GPT, Secure Boot and speed; the settings to master are boot order, SATA mode, virtualisation and Secure Boot.
Partition tables and file systems have hard limits that explain real-world behaviour (2 TiB MBR, 4 GiB FAT32).
A clean install follows a fixed routine, and the work is not finished until drivers, updates and a backup are done.
Virtual machines and live USBs are the safest places to practise and repair.

summary: Devices are identified by ports, labels, LEDs and the default IP printed on the sticker.
The star topology with a switch is standard; mesh needs n(n − 1)/2 links; bus is obsolete.
Sharing needs a private profile, discovery on, permissions set and a path such as \\PC\Notes.
Laser, inkjet, dot-matrix, thermal and 3D printers differ in mechanism, cost per page and best use.
Install the driver, print a test page, share through the Sharing tab or use a network printer with a fixed IP, then maintain on a schedule.

sections.title: Network design and building the lab topologies
Testing and diagnostics: the command toolkit
Troubleshooting common issues and the mini LAN/WLAN task

summary: An IPv4 address has a network part and a host part, split by the mask; private ranges are reused in every LAN.
Subnetting borrows host bits: a /26 gives four subnets of 62 hosts; the mask and block size follow from the prefix.
Routers and switches are configured from the console or a web page, and the configuration must be saved.
Access points need an SSID, WPA2/WPA3 security and a sensible channel; MAC filtering is not security.
Ping, tracert, ipconfig, netstat, arp, nslookup, route and netsh form the standard toolkit, applied in the diagnostic ladder.

units.title: Problem Solving Techniques
topics: The systematic approach: Identify, Test, Isolate, Fix, Verify

sections.title: The systematic approach: Identify, Test, Isolate, Fix, Verify

summary: Troubleshooting is a method, not guesswork: identify, test, isolate, fix and verify.
A visual inspection finds many faults at once: loose cables, damaged ports, swollen capacitors, dust.
The elimination method uses the minimum configuration and known good parts, one change at a time.
BIOS/UEFI messages, beep codes and POST codes name the subsystem; network faults are tackled from the inside out with ping and ipconfig.
A log turns each repair into reusable knowledge.

units.title: Maintenance and Upgrade
topics: Eight rules for maintenance and upgrades

sections.title: Eight rules for maintenance and upgrades

summary: Plan the upgrade with the board manual and tools such as CPU-Z, Speccy and the Crucial scanner; check socket, RAM type, PSU and space.
RAM must match type, speed and form factor, and runs best in dual channel; SSD upgrades use cloning and aligned partitions.
Preventive maintenance means cleaning with compressed air, a soft brush and isopropyl alcohol, fresh paste, careful battery use and tidy airflow.
Update firmware only when needed, and never interrupt it.
Monitor SMART, memory, temperatures and stability, and keep a log.
